records.note: A page is like a text bullet, except you can add an icon and a background that will be displayed when you zoom in on the bullet. It's a way to organize your bullets into categories. If you are not zoomed in, the icon will appear as a miniature next to the text

fields.text: Hello ***world***
They are the main information stored in your `.jsonl` files. Each bullet has its own type and fields that define certain characteristics of the type
For example, a callout bullet has a *level* field that can be success, info, ...
This type of representation allows bullets to have rich and customized formatting

Basically, your bullets are stored in `.jsonl` ([JSON Lines](https://jsonlines.org)) files. This means that each line of the file is a JSON object containing either a single bullet information or metadata from your notes

records.note: Simplified example of what a `.jsonl` file looks like in TreeWrite

fields.text:
{"id": "...", "type": "text",  ...} // Bullet 1
{"id": "...", "type": "code",  ...} // Bullet 2
{"id": "...", "type": "image", ...} // Bullet 3
{"type": "metadata", ...}           // Metadata

The `.jsonl` file follows an [append-only](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Append-only) structure. This means that adding, removing, and updating bullets or metadata never alters already written JSON objects

records.note: Demonstration of how the append-only works. We write the text "Hello" in a bullet, and then update it to "Hello world". Instead of updating the existing row, we append a new duplicate row with the updated fields. From now on, only the last line is counted by TreeWrite, and the previous ones are ignored

fields.text:
{"id": "123", "type": "text", "text": "Hello", ...}       // First edit
{"id": "123", "type": "text", "text": "Hello world", ...} // Second edit
Basic concepts of `.jsonl` files
Append-only structure
All bullets have base fields (like `id` and `type`) and extra fields specific to each bullet type
Metadata is an object that contains information such as settings (favorites, tags, ...)
The reason behind this decision is very simple: ***performance***

If we were to update the bullet line with the new values, we would have to rewrite the entire file with each edit. This is because the lines don't have a fixed byte length, so we can't update a JSON object in the middle of the file without updating everything else. But appending new data to a file in the file system is a cheap and fast operation
You might be thinking that this approach would eventually leave the file huge and with a lot of old data from the same bullet, and that's true
The condition that is verified is:
In summary, the append-only structure allows updates to your bullets to be made almost instantly, regardless of the number of bullets in your document

To resolve this, each edit validates whether the file is growing too large and should be cleaned up to contain only the most recent data. If that's the case, then the file is rewritten, now containing only the latest data
Why use a custom file format instead of a database (like SQLite)?
Some reasons to use a JSON Lines file instead of a pure JSON file:
Using an append-only structure, each edit appends to the end of the file instead of overwriting the entire file, making TreeWrite much more performant for large documents
A damaged line or crash does not corrupt the entire document
Diffs in Git are kept small, summarized in just a few lines

fields.text: Bullet types and metadata
Bullet types
Easy backup and synchronization with [[01M3CK4TT3EEMYQ55VSYQVCFZK|Git]]. Merge conflicts are resolved automatically

The assets are stored in the directory `./treewrite/{filename.jsonl}/assets` (relative to your `.jsonl` file)
Each of your documents will have its own unique asset directory, allowing for complete isolation between documents
You can request to delete assets that are no longer in use in your document
You can see the list of existing assets in your document in the sidebar
You can rename your assets, which renames all fields in all bullet points that reference them
You can delete a tag, which removes it from all bullets that reference it in the document
Tags are stored in your file's [[01M3QBV3HN2WCBY37F2CMRV4VC|metadata]]. Each bullet optionally has a [[01M3Q2E3J20NKRPCQFF6YJK5MC|list of tags]]
Renaming a tag does not change any of its references, as they reference the tag's ID and not its name
You can search for bullets with dates in the calendar

Dates themselves don't have any inherent semantic meaning; you define that. For example, a date in a checkbox bullet might indicate a task; one on a page bullet might indicate an upcoming trip, and so on
It's also possible to filter the calendar by bullets with specific [[01M3CKKTSAKT9DVE52BA7VV5K0]]. If you have, for example, a "Task" tag, you can filter by tasks in the current week
The date is an optional field [[01M3Q2E3J20NKRPCQFF6YJK5MC|stored in each bullet]]
It runs the Git installed on your system, so your SSH keys, credentials and `.gitconfig` work just like in the terminal
The settings are stored in the [[01M3QBV3HPV0ND9TWNJ6VGABAK|metadata]] of your document, so they travel with it to other machines
Setup
Open the settings and go to the Git section
If the file is not in a repository, TreeWrite can create one in its folder. Temporary files and the [[01M3CK4AA3MES7HVDZBMNQYHER|published site]] are added to `.gitignore`
If the branch has no remote, type its URL and TreeWrite adds it as `origin` and pushes the branch
Finally, turn on the sync of the file and choose a mode
Modes
**Sync** pulls the changes of other machines before pushing yours. Use it to edit the same document on more than one machine
**Backup** only pushes. Use it when a single machine edits the document. If the remote has changes this machine doesn't have, the sync is paused
When it syncs
Some time after your last change (1 minute by default)
Periodically, to bring in the changes of other machines (every 5 minutes by default)
When the document is opened
When you switch to another document or close TreeWrite
When you click the sync status and then *Sync now*
Only the open document is synced, and each commit includes only the document and its [[01M3CJQZTGBY1KNX195FMMDHA5]]
Merge conflicts
Conflicts are resolved automatically. Instead of merging the lines of the [[01M3CK4D608BX01BDWAWPSDR8G|.jsonl file]], TreeWrite merges the bullets one by one
A bullet changed on only one machine keeps that change
A bullet changed on both machines keeps the version of the current machine, and you are notified
An edit always wins over a removal, so nothing you wrote is lost
The settings in the metadata are merged the same way, one by one
Two different assets added with the same name on each machine are both kept. The one from the other machine gets a new name (like `photo-2.png`) and its references are updated
The result is appended to the file, keeping it [[01M3PN21SX7VYQZTVH1TSFBE25|append-only]]
Conflicts in other files of the repository are left to you. The merge is aborted, nothing is changed and the sync is paused
Sync status
The status is shown in the header, next to the save status. Clicking it shows the last sync time and a button to sync right away

rows: There are changes that were not pushed yet
The remote could not be reached. Your changes are committed and pushed once it is back
Something needs your attention, like a refused credential. Fix it and click *Retry*

fields.text: Click *Publish* in the header: TreeWrite builds the site and then runs a command of yours that uploads it wherever you want
The settings are stored in the [[01M3QBV3HHJ4CSRS185S2YD6TJ|metadata]] of your document
What is published
All the bullets of the document are published. Keep what is private in another document
Only the [[01M3CJQZTGBY1KNX195FMMDHA5]] referenced by bullets are copied to the site
From the metadata, only what the site needs to be drawn (theme, home, tags and sidebar features). The settings of Git and publish are never published
The sidebar of the site shows the same features that are on in the editor
How it works
The document is saved and the site is built in `./treewrite/{filename.jsonl}/publish` (relative to your `.jsonl` file)
The command runs inside that folder, in your login shell. You see its output as it runs and can cancel it at any time
Without a command, the site is only built. You can open its folder and upload it by hand
The folder is built from scratch on every publish, and only replaces the previous one once it is complete
The site is fully static and uses URLs like `/#/bullets/{id}`, so it works on any static host, even in a subfolder, with no extra configuration
Settings

rows: Uploads the site. It runs inside the site folder, also given by `TREEWRITE_PUBLISH_DIR`. `TREEWRITE_DOCUMENT` gives the `.jsonl` file
Where the site is found once published. It adds a picture of the home to link previews and a button to open the site after publishing

fields.text: The command can't ask for anything, like a password. Log in to your platform in the terminal once, or use an access token in an environment variable
Never write tokens in the command: it is stored in the file and goes to Git with it. Set them in your shell profile instead
Files the host needs in the folder (like a `CNAME`) must be created by the command, since the folder is built from scratch every time
Deploy tutorials
GitHub Pages
Put your document in a Git repository with a GitHub remote (see [[01M3CK4TT3EEMYQ55VSYQVCFZK]])
Use the command below. It pushes the site to the `gh-pages` branch of the repository

records.note: `CACHE_DIR` is needed because the site folder has no `package.json`. `--nojekyll` keeps GitHub from ignoring files that start with `_`. For a custom domain, add `--cname notes.example.com`

fields.text: CACHE_DIR="$HOME/.cache" npx gh-pages -d . --nojekyll
On GitHub, go to *Settings › Pages* and deploy from the `gh-pages` branch
Set the Site URL to `https://{user}.github.io/{repository}/`
Cloudflare Pages
Log in once with `npx wrangler login`, or set `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` in your shell profile
Create the project once with `npx wrangler pages project create notes --production-branch main`
Use the command below
npx wrangler pages deploy . --project-name notes --branch main
Set the Site URL to `https://notes.pages.dev/`
Netlify
Log in once with `npx netlify-cli login`, or set `NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN` in your shell profile
Create the site once with `npx netlify-cli sites:create --name notes`
Use the command below
npx netlify-cli deploy --dir . --prod --site notes
Set the Site URL to `https://notes.netlify.app/`
Your own server
Have an SSH key that doesn't ask for a passphrase, or one loaded in your SSH agent
Use the command below
rsync -az --delete ./ user@example.com:/var/www/notes/
Set the Site URL to the address your web server serves that folder at
Performance and memory
The whole document is loaded into memory while it is open, so the memory TreeWrite uses grows with the size of the document
Only the document being shown is loaded. The other open files take no memory until you switch to them
If a document gets too big, or mixes unrelated subjects, split it into several documents. Each one also has its own [[01M3CJQZTGBY1KNX195FMMDHA5]], settings and [[01M3CK4AA3MES7HVDZBMNQYHER|site]]
Writing faster
Type `/` at the start of a bullet to change its type

Or type at the start of the text, followed by Space: `#`, `##` or `###` for a title, `[]` for a checkbox, three backticks for code (type a language like `ts` right after them to set it) and `$$` for math
Type `[[` to reference another bullet, searching it by its text
*Shift+Enter* adds a note to the bullet
Inside code, math and tables, where *Tab* is taken, use *Ctrl+Tab* to indent the bullet and *Ctrl+Enter* to leave it
In the asset picker (of an image, a file or an icon), you can paste an image or a file copied in your file manager, or drag files into the window
Navigating
*Ctrl+F* searches the whole document, from anywhere
*Alt+←* and *Alt+→* go back and forth between the bullets you opened
*Ctrl+Space* expands or collapses everything inside the open bullet
*Ctrl+click* a reference to open it in a new tab. *Ctrl+1* to *Ctrl+9* switch between tabs, and the middle click closes them
Drag a bullet by its circle to move it anywhere in the view
Add the bullets you open the most to the favorites
The *Random bullet* button on the home is a good way to revisit old notes
Your file
Your document is a plain text file, so you can read it with any tool, like `jq` or a script of yours
Only change the file by hand while it is closed in TreeWrite, since the app keeps appending to it while it is open
Turn off the sidebar panels you don't use in *Settings › Features*. Nothing is lost: their data stays in the file
